why-organize-game-guides-again: Finding a game guide is easy these days.
Search for a game name together with a boss, map, collectible or quest, and an answer usually appears quickly. Videos, wikis, forums and community posts offer an ever-growing wealth of information.
But finding an answer and finding the answer needed right now are two different things.
Often, a player simply wants to know:
“Where do I go next from here?”
Yet the search result may be a complete walkthrough that starts at the beginning of the game.
A player missing just one collectible may have to work through dozens of item descriptions to find it.

The map is on one page, the boss on another, and ability unlocks scattered elsewhere. Each source may be perfectly useful on its own, but during play there is still a lot of switching, searching and interpreting to do.
GAME NOTE therefore aims to do more than simply add another guide:
It aims to organize complex game information clearly.
This matters especially in exploration-focused games.
A new ability opens areas that were previously inaccessible.
A collectible that cannot be reached yet may only become available several hours later.
A place that looks nearby on the map may require a long detour to reach.
For games like these, simply arranging everything into Chapter One, Chapter Two and Chapter Three may not make information easy to find.
A guide needs to answer additional questions.
Should an ability be documented in the walkthrough, in the ability list, or both?
Besides marking a collectible’s location, should the guide explain when it becomes obtainable?
Should a map contain every possible detail, or focus on the important nodes?
Should a boss page explain only combat tactics, or also its relationship to the areas before and after it?
These may look like questions about website structure, but they all lead to the same goal:
“Standing here right now, what does the player most need to know?”
GAME NOTE does not want to become a website that merely has a lot of articles.
The number of guides is not what matters.
What matters is that a player who is stuck can open a page without first having to learn how the website works.
Where is the map?
Where should the player go next?
When does this ability become available?
What needs attention in this boss fight?
Which items remain inaccessible for now and can be revisited later?
When this information is easy to find, a guide has truly done the work of organizing it.
Publishing a page does not mean that work is finished.
A route may still need adjustment.
Map markers may be made clearer.
A step may be technically correct and still difficult to understand.
Pages therefore continue to be revised through actual use.
Rather than being the first guide published, GAME NOTE hopes to preserve a game archive that becomes clearer through continued organization.
Perhaps the real value of a guide is not having more information, but saving players a few detours while looking for it.
why-an-jing-wei-guang-looks-like-an-old-: Modern guide websites tend to follow a well-established design language.
Large images, cards, clear categories, responsive layouts and increasingly streamlined navigation.
There is nothing wrong with these choices.
But while preparing the Well Dweller guide, another, now uncommon kind of website began to feel appealing again:
The Chinese game-specific guide sites of twenty years ago.
By today’s design standards, those sites were not especially polished.
Pages were often narrow.
A long directory ran down the left side.
Chapter headings might simply be conspicuous red text.
Relatively small screenshots appeared among the walkthrough paragraphs.
Bosses, items, magic and maps were often organized directly into colorful tables.
At the bottom of the page, navigation might be nothing more than:
“Previous | Contents | Next”
There were no elaborate animations.
No hero section occupying an entire screen.
And no giant card appearing every few paragraphs.
Yet this structure had one very direct advantage:
After opening the page, it was easy to see what was available.
The left-hand directory ran from systems to walkthroughs, maps, bosses, secrets and collectibles.
It could even look a little dense.
But that density gave players a clear first impression:
“The information for this game is all organized here.”
Many websites now hide more information in pursuit of visual simplicity.
Three entry points become three large cards.
Additional sections move into secondary menus.
A screen shows only a small amount of content.
For a general-purpose website, that may feel more modern.
But a guide site does not necessarily need to work that way.
When a game contains many maps, bosses, items and secrets, the amount of information does not need to be concealed.
The real challenge is making that information easy to find even when there is a lot of it.
The Well Dweller guide will therefore revisit some traditional guide-site design methods.
A complete directory kept visible on the left, for example.
Clear, direct text links.
And familiar markers:
★ Main route · ◆ Important collectibles · ※ Cautions · → Next step
The body will not be turned entirely into modern cards.
Walkthroughs remain article-led, with screenshots appearing naturally among the text.
Information that a table explains well—boss details, item locations or requirements—will be presented in tables.
Page navigation returns to the simplest form:
“Previous / Contents / Next”
These elements retain part of the traditional guide-site reading experience.
Of course, this does not mean literally rebuilding a website from twenty years ago.
Text will not be too small to read.
Page width will not be fixed for old monitors.
On phones, the long directory moves into a separate guide menu.
Images adapt to the screen.
Wide tables scroll within their own container instead of breaking the page.
SEO, responsiveness, HTML structure and loading performance still follow modern website practices.
A more accurate description of the design is therefore:
“Traditional guide-site reading, built on a modern website.”
The theme is called:
GAME NOTE CLASSIC
It is not only about nostalgia.
More importantly, this kind of structure is well suited to long game guides.
When a game has many areas, bosses, collectibles and systems, a guide site can sometimes say plainly:
“There is a lot of content here.”
While also giving players confidence:
“What you need should be somewhere in this directory.”
That sense of certainty is part of the guide experience.
Well Dweller will be the first guide to use GAME NOTE CLASSIC.
It is also among the first new additions as GAME NOTE moves from separate guide subdomains into a unified game directory.
A new technical structure paired with a very old reading style.
Perhaps that is a good fit for a game guide.
mapping-a-metroidvania: A map is not finished when every room has been drawn. It needs to explain where the player is, what is missing and what routes are possible next.
Area names are not always the most effective entry point. A landmark in a screenshot, a newly obtained ability, a door or a mechanism often better matches the question a player brings.
Ability requirements matter more than completion percentages.
A useful map clearly distinguishes places that can be reached now from places to revisit later, reducing aimless backtracking.
A map should lead to the relevant walkthrough, boss and collectible pages, while those pages should lead back to the map. This two-way relationship is more useful than an isolated large image.
after-islets: Boss tactics can often be explained on their own. The more complicated problem is moving from one area to the next with incomplete clues.
Different questions on the same map.
A first visit, a return after obtaining a new ability and a collectible cleanup run do not need the same answers. The walkthrough must distinguish them.
Instead of naming only a place, provide visible landmarks, the immediate objective and ability requirements. Players should not need to identify their chapter before they can continue.
